title: Somebody Else's Rope
logline: On a wide brown river with no bridge for several miles a wire runs bank to bank, and all day people put their hands on it and haul themselves and their bicycles across, arriving on the far side under their own weight, on a line none of them put up and most of them could not name the maker of.
human_question: If you got yourself across, and nothing came with you, what exactly is it that arrived?

place.what_kind_of_place: A reach of a large lowland river in the wet south-west, brown with silt, sixty or eighty metres across, running between low banks of red clay under rubber, coconut and jak, with a gravel road ending on each side at a worn slope into the water. There is no bridge here. Across the river there is a wire or a heavy rope, anchored at each end to a tree or a driven post, sagging into the middle, sometimes wet, sometimes with grass and river weed caught on it. On the water there is a flat craft — planks over a hull, or two hulls decked over — open, unpainted, with a rubbing strip along one edge from decades of hands and hulls, big enough for perhaps a dozen people and their loads, or one motorcycle, or a bicycle and a sack of something. There is a shelter of sorts on one bank, a bench, a pole for the rope, and the two landings: bare clay, cut into steps by feet, rebuilt after every high water. Above and below, the river is empty.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because the thing the place does, it does about a hundred times a day, and because the whole mechanism is visible in one frame. From directly above, the picture is almost a diagram and is beautiful before it means anything: a broad brown band, a single straight line drawn across it, and a small dark rectangle sliding along the line. From the bank at eye level it is a study of hands and weight: people take hold of a wire above their heads, lean, walk the length of the deck, come back, take hold again, and the far bank arrives. And there is one thing the camera can do here that it can do almost nowhere else. It can hold the near bank, in one locked frame, from the moment the craft pushes off to the moment it lands, and show that the near bank is not diminished, not moved, not altered, and that nothing at all has left it — while the crossing depended on it absolutely. The most beautiful shot the place produces is also, without a word being said, the entire argument.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The river, constantly, and the arrangement, hardly at all. The water level moves through the year and the crossing changes character with it: slack and easy in the dry months, hard and fast after rain, and impossible in flood, when the wire goes under and the landings disappear. The rope is spliced, moved, tightened and replaced without ceremony, and nobody on the deck at any given moment is the person who put it there. The traffic changes with the hour: school times, market times, the end of a shift, and long slack middles when the craft lies on one bank and nothing happens for twenty minutes. Over years the crossing is on a clock of its own: every such crossing in the country either gets a bridge and stops, or loses its people and stops. The film has no event to wait for. It has a repetition and a river.
place.when_it_looks_best: The drier months, when the water is low enough that the crossing runs all day and the wire is above the surface, and when the air is clear enough to get height. The first and last hours give low sun across the water and long reflections of the wire, and they coincide with the two busiest parts of the day. The middle of the day is worth filming for the opposite reason: flat light, empty deck, nobody waiting, and the line across the river doing nothing at all. The first weeks of the monsoon are worth one visit for the fast water and the rain, but not for the flood itself, which stops the subject rather than intensifying it.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film about a river with no bridge and the line that is strung across it. The reach from above at first light; the two clay landings cut into steps by feet; a wire rising out of the water, its anchor tree, its splice, the weed caught on it; hands going along it hand over hand; a bicycle held upright on a moving deck; a schoolbag, a sack, a motorcycle wheeled up a slope; long empty middles of the day when nothing crosses; the wake going flat; rain arriving up the river; the last crossing in the dark. It has a complete shape with nothing said over it: a gap, a line, and a hundred ordinary arrivals. Anyone who likes water, working objects or the sight of a whole mechanism at once has a whole piece here.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same day becomes the sources' own picture for how one moment of a life gives rise to the next, filmed at the only place where that picture is a piece of infrastructure. The older commentary explains the link between one existence and the next with a man who crosses a stream on a rope tied to a tree on the near bank, and who comes to rest on the far side by his own weight, whether or not there is anything tied to a tree on that side, with nothing at all having come over from the bank he left. The voice says plainly that this is the source's illustration and not the film's invention. And it says what the passage is for: not that everything is connected, but that dependence here is total and transfer is nil, and that it runs one way. The bank gives; it does not receive. Nobody strung the line for the people now on it. Nobody is working the crossing from outside it.

sequence.on_screen: First light, high and straight down. A broad brown river between low banks of trees. A single taut line drawn across it from one bank to the other. Two bare clay landings, each at the end of a gravel road that simply stops.
sequence.voice: There is no bridge on this river for some miles. There is a wire, and there is a flat craft, and all day people take hold of the wire and pull themselves across. Nobody now waiting on this bank put the wire up.

sequence.on_screen: Eye level on the near bank. The craft nosed into the clay. Hands reaching up and closing on the wire. Weight going back. The bank beginning to move in frame.
sequence.voice: The older commentary explains the link between one existence and the next with a picture, and this is the picture, in their words and not ours: like a man who crosses a stream holding a rope tied to a tree on the near bank [C080-P:L937–L943].

sequence.on_screen: The far landing. A bicycle wheeled off, a bag lifted, feet finding the clay steps. The craft drifting back against its line. Nobody looking back.
sequence.voice: The passage finishes the picture exactly. He comes to a stand on the far bank by his own force, whether or not he gets hold of anything tied to a tree on that side [C080-P:L943]. And it says what it is refusing: that there is no travelling from the earlier state to this one, and no crossing over of anybody from one existence into another [C080-P:L929–L931].

sequence.on_screen: A locked frame on the near bank, held long. The craft leaves the bottom of the shot, crosses, lands. The clay, the steps, the anchor post and the grass are exactly as they were. Nothing has gone.
sequence.voice: They put the same point four more ways: an echo, a lamp lit from a lamp, a seal pressed into wax, a face in a mirror. In each of them, they say, the result stands where it was produced and has not gone anywhere else [C080-P:L945].

sequence.on_screen: The wire itself at arm's length: the anchor tree with old bark growth over an older loop, a splice, wear, weed, a section under water. Then the same wire from height, drawn straight across the frame.
sequence.voice: So the arrangement runs one way, and it matters that the film says so rather than saying everything holds everything up. This bank supplies the whole condition of the crossing and receives nothing back from it. The sources refuse both easy readings at once: if the two were simply identical, curd could not come out of milk; if they were simply separate, curd would have nothing to do with milk at all [C080-P:L955].

sequence.on_screen: Crossing after crossing through a middle stretch of the day: different loads, different people, the same line, the same two slopes. Then twenty minutes of nothing, the craft tied up, the wire still.
sequence.voice: The other book holds two ways of looking at this together, on purpose. Seen only as continuity, it looks like something unchanging running the whole length of it, the way a seed becomes a tree, and that reading hardens into a permanent self. Seen only as difference, each stage looks unrelated to the last, and that reading hardens into the idea that nothing carries on at all. Each correction is what the other one needs [C081-P:L523–L548].

sequence.on_screen: Rain coming up the river. Fast brown water, the wire wet, the crossing harder and still happening. Then the last crossing of the day in the dark, and the empty craft against the bank.
sequence.voice: One thing this is not. The method the sources call non-agency says that not-seeing does not think, I shall produce intention; intention does not think, we shall produce awareness [C081-P:L541–L545]. There is no maker behind the arrangement and no self inside it doing the acting or collecting the results [C080-P:L1619]. It is not a system of reward and punishment run by anybody. The wire does not know anyone is on it.

concept_merge.why_together: C080 supplies the film's whole spine, and it supplies it as the source's own image rather than as anything a film-maker invented. The Pradeepika explains rebirth-linking with a man crossing a stream on a rope tied to a tree on the near bank, and it completes the image by saying that he comes to a stand on the far side by his own force whether or not he finds anything tied to a tree there [C080-P:L937–L943]. It states in as many words that there is no travelling from the earlier existence to this one and no passing over of a person from one to another, and that in the ultimate sense there is no being and no self [C080-P:L929–L931]. It offers four more pictures for the same point, the echo, the lamp, the seal and the reflection, and insists that the result stands where it was produced and has gone nowhere [C080-P:L945]. And it holds the middle position with an argument rather than a mood: if the two were absolutely identical, curd could not arise from milk; if absolutely different, curd would have no connection with milk, and the same reasoning applies to seed and shoot [C080-P:L955]. C081 supplies the frame that stops the image from being enjoyed. Its four methods are set out as a matched set in which each corrective produces a new error if it is taken alone: continuity seen rightly gives up annihilationism and seen wrongly hardens into eternalism; difference seen rightly gives up eternalism and seen wrongly hardens into annihilationism; and non-agency, seen rightly, drops the idea of a self by understanding that there is no maker such as a supreme god behind any of it [C081-P:L523–L548; C081-P:L541–L545]. A working crossing on a rope somebody else strung is the first concept as a physical fact and the second as the reason to keep the camera on the mechanism rather than on the crossing's mood.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That dependence can be total and transfer nil, and that this is a statement about order and direction rather than about belonging. The doctrine said flat sounds like a paradox to be admired. Filmed here it is a locked shot: the bank supplies everything the crossing needs, nothing leaves the bank, the arrival happens under the arriver's own weight, and the whole of it depends on a line put up by somebody who is not present and may be dead. The film also gets the group's hardest guard rail for nothing, because the arrangement is visibly one-directional: a viewer can see that this is not a web and not a mutual embrace, and the voice can say so without arguing. The idea was previously marked for merger into the roof film on the grounds that it required a simile to be acted out in front of the camera. That reading is reversed here. The crossing is not an enactment: it is a hundred real arrivals a day at a place where the source's own illustration happens to be the local transport, and the film's job is to stop centring the person who works it and start filming the line, the two banks and the weight.

concept_links.why: Four of the digest's statements are narrated and each is anchored to something the lens is already on. The rope-and-tree image is spoken over hands closing on the wire and named out loud as the source's picture [C080-P:L937–L943], and its completion, that the man stands on the far bank by his own force whether or not anything is tied there, is spoken over the far landing [C080-P:L943]. The refusal of transfer is spoken over the same landing, in the source's own terms of no travelling and no passing over, and with its denial of a being or a self attached rather than softened [C080-P:L929–L931]. The echo, lamp, seal and mirror are spoken over the one locked shot that proves the point, a near bank unchanged after a crossing [C080-P:L945]. And the milk-and-curd argument is spoken over the wire itself, because that is where the film states its direction [C080-P:L955]. Every limit in the digest that bears on this film is honoured, and two of them are the closing beat. 'Everything is connected' as a warm slogan is refused structurally: the film says the bank gives and receives nothing, and the group's own title is treated as the error the digest names twice. Rebirth as a soul moving into a body is refused out loud, which matters more here than anywhere, because a crossing is exactly the picture that invites it. 'What goes around comes around' is refused by saying there is no judge and no system of payback. 'You create your own reality' is refused by the same beat, which denies a self who acts or experiences. Ignorance is never presented as lack of schooling and is not glossed at all. The cosmology, the death-moment material, the account of what the dying mind takes as its object, and the hells and heavens are not narrated, alluded to or implied anywhere: nobody in this film is dying, and no crossing stands for a death. The film also never suggests that the people crossing are illustrations of anything, and it does not read the tradition as anticipating anything about rivers.

The digest's four methods are used as a matched set and not as an ornament. The beat over the repeated crossings states both of the first two and, crucially, states the digest's structural point that each method prevents one error and produces another when taken alone: continuity alone suggests something unchanging running through, difference alone suggests no relation [C081-P:L523–L548]. Non-agency carries the closing beat, in the source's own terms, that not-seeing does not intend to produce intention and that seeing this rightly means understanding there is no maker [C081-P:L541–L545]. Every limit in the digest is honoured. 'My soul is reborn' is the reading the film most has to guard against and it is refused explicitly. 'Life is a beautiful circle' is refused by keeping the film to one reach of one river and one repeated mechanism, with no circle anywhere in it and nothing celebrated. 'What goes around comes around' as cosmic justice is refused by the non-agency beat in as many words. The claim that not-seeing is an origin is avoided entirely, since the film makes no claim about beginnings and the digest is explicit that both books deny a first one. The three-period frame, the twenty modes, the four groups and the two roots are not narrated: they would need a diagram, not footage, and the film does not gesture at them. Past-life psychology is nowhere in the film.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That in this analysis one state of a life gives rise to the next without anything at all travelling across, the way an arrival on a far bank depends wholly on the bank behind and takes nothing of it; that the tradition refuses both the idea of something unchanging making the journey and the idea that the two ends are unrelated, and gives an argument rather than a mood for that middle position; and that no one is running the arrangement and nobody is being paid back by it. The crossing is the source's own illustration and the film says so; no claim is made about anybody on the water.
what_must_be_real: The crossing as it is used, at the hours it is used. No trip is arranged, no crossing is repeated for a second angle, nobody is asked to take hold of the rope again, and no crossing is emptied of ordinary passengers so that a frame looks better. Nothing about the craft, the rope, the anchors or the landings is cleaned, tightened, repaired or repositioned for the camera. The person who works the crossing is filmed as one of the people present and is not made into the film's subject, a character or a figure of pathos, and is not asked to confirm or comment on any doctrine. Children crossing to school are not filmed identifiably without their guardians' and their school's agreement. Nobody is filmed in a way that shows what they carry, what they paid or where they live. If the water is high enough that a crossing is unsafe, the film does not go on the water.
position_hint: middle, immediately after the group's plain forward statement of the chain and before the film that takes continuity across years. It is the group's first film about carrying-on rather than about steps in a day, and it is the right place to say out loud, on the simplest possible mechanism, that dependence running one way is not the same as everything holding everything up. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Letting the crossing be read as a soul making a journey, which is the exact view the source rejects and which this image invites more strongly than any other in the group.
Celebrating interconnection, when the arrangement on screen is one-directional and the source's own digest rejects the warm reading twice.
Centring the person who works the crossing, so that the film becomes a portrait of a disappearing livelihood and the concept becomes its caption.
Sentimentalising a lack of infrastructure, or implying that a community is better off without a bridge.
Letting the rope become a mystery and the crossing a ritual, when it is a wire, a splice and a set of hands.
Filming schoolchildren's daily crossing as picturesque, or identifiably without consent.
Making the film look like an enactment of a simile, with the mechanism arranged to match a text.
Putting anyone at risk on fast water for a shot, or implying that a hard crossing is more interesting than an easy one.
drop_if: No hand-hauled crossing is still working on this river, and none can be found in the district, since the whole film is the mechanism.
The crossing has been replaced by an engine, so nobody arrives under their own effort and the source's image is no longer on screen.
The only way to film a crossing is to commission one.
Height over the reach cannot be obtained at all, so the one shot that carries the argument, the whole mechanism in a single frame, cannot be made.

connections.note: Two films on continuity with nothing carried across: one at the scale of a single arrival that takes a minute, one at the scale of a covering that is wholly replaced and still called the same thing.
One follows a chain forward through a day that cannot be reordered; this one stops on a single joint in it and asks what passes across the joint, and answers nothing.

selection.reason: The source's own illustration for this concept happens to be a working piece of transport, and the single most beautiful shot the place produces, the whole mechanism from directly above, is also the concept stated without words.

review.note: Rewritten 2026-09-24 into the footage-led shape, and un-merged. The previous version was marked for merger into the roof film on the grounds that it depended on a simile being acted out in front of the camera; that judgement is reversed, because a working crossing is not an enactment and the roof film cannot carry both concepts at full weight. What was dropped from the old version: the person who works the crossing as the film's subject, the livelihood-under-threat framing, and the community's dependence on the crossing as the stake. What is kept and sharpened: the source's own rope image, and the point that dependence can be complete while transfer is nil. The film now centres the line, the two banks and the weight, and the person working it appears as one of the people present. Both digests were re-read from scratch and every citation was verified line by line against the source files; the old idea carried no citations at all. The group's own title was treated as its central trap: the film states that the arrangement runs one way, and the closing beat carries the corrections about a maker, about a self and about payback.

suggested_location.name: The hand-hauled crossing of the Kalu Ganga at Palam Paruwa, below Ingiriya, Kalutara District

also_known_as.name: paruwa
also_known_as.meaning: the flat plank craft itself, and by extension the crossing; the place name Palam Paruwa carries both the word for a bridge and the word for the craft

also_known_as.name: totupola
also_known_as.meaning: a landing or ferry place; most such crossings are recorded under a totupola name on each bank
also_known_as.used_by: Sinhala usage and the ferry schedules of the colonial gazettes

also_known_as.name: Kalu Ganga
also_known_as.meaning: the black river, which rises in the central hills and reaches the sea in this district after about a hundred and thirty kilometres

suggested_location.region: Kalutara District, Western Province: the reach of the district's main river along the southern edge of the inland town at the meeting of the hill and coastal roads, between rubber and coconut land, upstream of the wide tidal lower river
suggested_location.why_here: Because this district's main river has carried hand-hauled crossings along its whole middle length for as long as there are records of them, and because this particular reach is where a crossing of exactly this kind is attested by name: a place recorded as Palam Paruwa on this river, in the area of the inland town whose southern boundary the river forms. The colonial ferry schedules list a run of crossings on this river and its tributaries in this district, and the one crossing on that list whose working method is described in as many words is hand-hauled: a steel rope strung across the river and all the passengers pulling on it. That is the whole film in one sentence, and it is the source's own image in one sentence as well. The reach itself is right for the camera: a wide brown river with low clay banks under rubber and coconut, roads that end at the water on both sides, and no bridge for some distance, so the crossing has an obvious function and the line across the river is legible from height. The district is also one of the thinnest on this slate, and this is a working piece of everyday transport rather than a ceremony, an institution or anybody's grief.
what_to_film: The reach from directly above at first light and at last light, so the river, the single line across it and the small rectangle sliding along it read as one picture.
One crossing end to end in a single take at eye level, from the near landing to the far one, with the hands on the wire the only thing in the frame that is working.
A locked frame on the near bank, held from push-off to landing, in which the bank is visibly unaltered by the crossing. This is the shot the film exists for.
The wire and its anchors at arm's length: bark grown over an old loop, a splice, wear, weed caught on it, and the section that goes under water.
The two landings in detail: clay cut into steps by feet, ruts from bicycle wheels, the mark of the craft's edge, and the rebuilding after high water if it falls inside the window.
Loads crossing without comment: a bicycle, a sack, a motorcycle, a bundle of cut rubber wood, somebody's chair.
A long empty middle of the day: the craft tied up, the road ending at the water, nothing happening, and the line still there.
Rain arriving up the river, and a crossing made in fast water, filmed from the bank and not from the deck.
The upstream and downstream views from the same point, to establish that there is nothing else to use.
suggested_location.access: By road from either the coast or the hill road to the inland town, and then on a minor road that ends at the water. Everything depends on whoever operates the crossing agreeing and on the people using it agreeing, and the film should not go on the water at all unless the operator is content that it can be done without changing how the crossing is worked. This is a river with a serious flood record in this district, so the water level has to be checked before travelling and the crossing may simply be out of use. Drone flight over a working river crossing with people on it needs the operator's agreement as well as any clearance required, and the elevated shots may have to be taken from a bank position rather than over the craft. If schoolchildren use the crossing at the hours the film wants, their school and guardians have to be approached before any identifiable filming.
suggested_location.best_time: The drier months, when the water is low enough for the crossing to run all day and clear enough for height: within a day, the first and last hours, which are also the busiest, and deliberately a slack middle hour for the empty deck. A single short visit early in the north-east monsoon is worth planning for the fast water and the rain, but not the flood itself, which stops the subject. The film wants two or three days rather than one, because the whole subject is repetition.

A picture of the named place on the river rather than a verified record of a hand-hauled crossing in use; what the frame actually contains has not been checked beyond its own caption.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, and unverified on the ground. From the sources above: a compiled list drawn from a 1954 gazette of ferries names a series of crossings on this district's main river and its tributaries, and describes one of them as little better than a raft of planks taking one vehicle at a time, worked by a steel rope strung across the river which all the passengers pull on; that particular crossing is recorded as having since been bridged, and several others on the list are noted as uncertain in location or status. The place name used here, Palam Paruwa, is attached to a photograph of this river filed under the name of the inland town whose southern boundary the river forms, and that town is recorded as being in this district at the meeting of the hill, coastal and inland roads. The coordinates are a direction towards the river reach below that town, not a survey: no landing, craft, rope, operator or household has been identified or approached. The single thing the film depends on — that a hand-hauled crossing is still working on this river, at this reach or nearby, without an engine — is an inference from the ferry list and from the place name, and has not been confirmed by anybody. If it is not working here, the same list gives two further crossings on this river and its tributaries in this district to check before the idea is dropped. No permission has been sought from any operator, school or authority, and no photograph confirming a hand-hauled crossing at this place was found on Wikimedia Commons; the two images are of the named place on the river and of the same river further upstream in another district.

unknowns: Whether a hand-hauled crossing is still working anywhere on this river in this district, and whether it is worked on a rope or on an engine. This is the question that decides whether the film exists.
Whether the craft is pulled by the passengers themselves or only by an operator, since the film's central claim is that people arrive under their own effort.
Who operates the crossing, who has to agree, and whether a camera can be on the water without altering how it is worked.
Whether height can be obtained over a working crossing with people on it, and from where.
How the crossing behaves across a year, and whether an accessible window exists between the flood season and the low water that might strand it.
Whether the hours the film wants are school hours, and what consent that requires.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is proposed by Claude from desk research and is unverified. No scene or shot is decided here.
